children: The generations-old higher-education business model is under growing pressure. Even brand-name institutions like Syracuse University, a midsize private school, are starting to feel the heat. Here are five things to know about the challenges facing Syracuse and others.

In 2007, Americans had more babies than any other year in the nation's history. Then came the 2008 financial crisis and a growing number of young people felt priced out of parenthood. First felt in the Midwest and Northeast, that decline in birthrates is now hitting campuses nationwide. By 2041, the number of traditional-age college students is projected to fall 13%, according to the Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education.

That decline is exacerbated by a drop in the percentage of students who are choosing college right out of high school. In 2016, 70% of students went straight to a two- or four-year college, according to federal data. That rate fell to 62% by 2022, the last year for which data is available.

President Trump started cracking down on international student enrollment last year by tightening visa restrictions and limiting job opportunities. This past fall, the number of new international students enrolling in American schools fell 17%, according to a report in part by the Institute of International Education.

This decline hurts because international students often pay the full price of tuition and, in some cases, additional fees. A majority of domestic students at most schools receive some type of financial aid from the university.

A growing number of Americans are fleeing the north for the south for college, making it harder for some northern schools to fill classes. Students are motivated by better weather, less political activism, stronger local economies and the school spirit of southern flagship universities.
At the same time, there is a migration of students to public universities from private and for-profit schools, according to the National Student Clearinghouse Research Center.

In 2019, the U.S. Justice Department abolished the gentleman's agreement between colleges to end negotiations with prospective students over financial-aid packages after May 1. Now schools regularly make last-minute offers through the summer to poach students who have accepted offers at other colleges.

This phenomenon has empowered families to demand steeper discounts and generate bidding wars between schools. It has also become increasingly difficult for schools to predict how many students will show up for the start of the school year.

In July, the Trump administration capped graduate-school borrowing at $100,000, and borrowing for professional degrees at $200,000. The caps aim to help curb the cost of attendance and slow the rise of student debt, which is now at a record $1.7 trillion. The changes could threaten enrollment at some graduate programs that have long been a source of revenue for universities.
